message.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
	  <jats:p>We present the first radio–continuum detection of the circumstellar shell around the well-known WN8 type Wolf-Rayet star WR16 at 943.5 MHz using the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP) Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) survey. At this frequency, the shell has a measured flux density of 72.2<jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline1.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$\pm$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula>7.2 mJy. Using previous Australia Telescope Compact Array (ATCA) measurements at 2.4, 4.8, and 8.64 GHz, as well as the Evolutionary Map of the Universe (EMU) observations of the star itself, we determine a spectral index of <jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline2.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$\alpha\,=\,+0.74\pm0.02$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula>, indicating thermal emission. We propose that the shell and star both exhibit thermal emission, supported by the its appearance in near-infrared and H<jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline3.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$\alpha$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula> observations. The latest <jats:italic>Gaia</jats:italic> parallax is used to determine a distance of 2.28<jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline4.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$\pm$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula>0.09 kpc. This star is well known for its surrounding circular nebulosity, and using the distance and an angular diameter of <jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline5.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$8.^{\prime}42$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula>, we determine the shell size to be 5.57<jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline6.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$\pm$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula>0.22 pc. We use the <jats:italic>Gaia</jats:italic> proper motion (PM) of WR16 to determine peculiar velocities of the star as <jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline7.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$V_{\alpha}(pec) =$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula> –45.3<jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline8.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$\pm$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula>5.4 km s<jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline9.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$^{-1}$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula> and <jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline10.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$V_{\delta}(pec) =$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula> 22.8<jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline11.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$\pm$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula>4.7 km s<jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline12.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$^{-1}$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula>, which indicates that the star is moving in a north-west direction, and translates to a peculiar tangential velocity to be 50.7<jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline13.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$\pm$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula>6.9 km s<jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline14.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$^{-1}$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula>. We also use these proper motion (PM) to determine the shell’s origin, estimate an age of <jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline15.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$\sim 9500\pm 1300$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula> yr, and determine its average expansion velocity to be <jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline16.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$280\pm40$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula> km s<jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline17.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$^{-1}$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula>. This average expansion velocity suggests that the previous transitional phase is a Luminous Blue Variable (LBV) phase, rather than a Red Super Giant (RSG) phase. We also use the measured flux at 943.5 MHz to determine a mass-loss rate of <jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline18.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$1.753\times 10^{-5}\,{\rm M}_\odot\,$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula>yr<jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline19.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$^{-1}$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula>, and use this to determine a lower-limit on ionising photons of <jats:inline-formula>
	      <jats:alternatives>
		<jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" mime-subtype="png" xlink:href="S1323358025100702_inline20.png"/>
		<jats:tex-math>
$N_{UV} \gt 1.406\times 10^{47}\,\textit{s}^{-1}$
</jats:tex-math>
	      </jats:alternatives>
	    </jats:inline-formula>.</jats:p>
title: Evolutionary map of the Universe: Detection and analysis of the shell surrounding the runaway Wolf-Rayet star WR16
